articles.body:
November 24, 2026

Pharmacies in Iran are closing, hospital deliveries have stalled and patients are rationing doses or turning to black markets.

Ahmad,* 67, visited nearly 20 Tehran pharmacies for the antipsychotic drug chlorpromazine, but left empty-handed.

"When a patient has to go to this many pharmacies just to find an essential drug, you really have to ask who is responsible for supplying medicine," he told DW.

Mitra,* a 37-year-old Tehran resident with diabetes , spent days hunting for insulin. "These are not drugs I can postpone taking or simply give up," she said. "My life depends on regular access to this insulin."

Their ordeal reflects a wider crisis across Iran's health care system.

Along with Tehran residents, DW spoke with an official at Iran's Food and Drug Administration (IFDA) and pharmacy workers in Tehran, Rasht and Mahabad. The interviews were conducted anonymously or using pseudonyms as speaking with foreign media remains dangerous in Iran.

Iran's broken drug supply chain

The official said that Iran's falling currency, along with price controls, has drained domestic drugmaker profits, while unpaid hospital debts have delayed deliveries.

"Add our own hospitals' heavy unpaid debts to distributors, and you can see why distribution has ground to a halt and companies are no longer supplying hospitals," the official said.

"Unless the Plan and Budget Organization makes our currency allocation realistic, banks step in with loans for drugmakers and insurers settle their debts, the Health Ministry's hands will remain tied and this disaster cannot be stopped," the official warned.

IFDA spokesman Mohammad Hashemi told Iran's semi-official ILNA news agency on November 9 that fewer than 40 of roughly 700 essential drugs faced supply difficulties. However, pharmacists told DW about how difficult it can be to get drugs on shelves.

A pharmacy manager in Tehran said insurance payments are often delayed by months, while drug prices continue to climb. Another pharmacist in the northwestern Mahabad region said distributors demand cash upfront for scarce items.

The insurance delays and shifting rules have pushed some pharmacies to drop contracts or refuse costly insured drugs.

The pharmacist in Mahabad, who prefers to be called Leili,* said that general pharmacies can lack about 40 items, and larger specialty pharmacies stocking chemotherapy and complex treatments can lack over 100, including psychiatric and Parkinson's drugs, and insulin vials.

"Many drugs can no longer be found in the official supply chain at all, such as nimodipine tablets [used to treat certain strokes] or hospital injectable antibiotics that have no substitutes," she said.

Turning to low-quality, black market medicine

As common items like cold medication become scarcer or more expensive, some people are turning to home remedies, she said. She added that for essential medicines like insulin, chronic patients are using smaller doses to preserve supply.

Many of those unable to pay are middle-class customers whom pharmacists cannot easily refer to charities, she said, with elderly and psychiatric patients among the hardest hit.

Leili warned that lower quality seen in some reverse-engineered domestic drugs presents a high risk for cancer, transplant and autoimmune patients.

She added that some families are forced to turn to street markets usually located outside of clinics, which lack cold-chain controls and sell counterfeit medicines or drugs with altered expiration dates.

Another pharmacy manager who asked to be called Khadiv* said scarce medicines can fetch up to 10 times their official price.

Sanctions and blockades

Amid the current conflict with the US, Khadiv said US sanctions, along with border disruptions and the US maritime blockade in the Strait of Hormuz inflate import costs.

In a statement, the US State Department told DW its sanctions follow international law to deny Tehran funds for "destabilizing behavior," stressing the measures allow "broad authorizations and exceptions" for food, medicine and medical devices. It pointed to what it called Iran's "corrupt ruling elite" for not properly allocating resources.

Iranian officials, however, reject that claim. In late summer, Health Minister Mohammad Reza Zafarghandi called US exemption claims "a big lie," saying banking, insurance, flight and shipping sanctions block imports.

Earlier this fall, the IFDA's raw materials chief cited currency, banking, customs and shipping hurdles as the main bottleneck.

DW emailed the Iranian Embassy's media office in Berlin for comment but received no reply.

"Seeing so many people unable to afford their medicine or reach medical centers leaves me with a sense of guilt and helplessness," Khadiv said, adding that lack of access can even lead to patient deaths.

For patients like Ahmad and Mitra, the standoff offers no relief, and every day, the gap between official assurances and what is actually on pharmacy shelves grows harder to ignore.

*Names changed for safety reasons.

articles.title: UK invokes ‘British values’ in latest Houthi sanctions, makes no mention of ally Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: UK invokes ‘British values’ in latest Houthi sanctions, makes no mention of ally Saudi Arabia Britain has imposed fresh sanctions on Yemen’s Houthis, accusing the group of “serious human rights abuses” and efforts to “undermine” Middle Eastern stability. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband linked the measures to attacks on merchant vessels in Bab al-Mandeb, saying they had “driven up the cost of living at home”. He said the sanctions sent a “clear message” that Britain would “act in support of British values and interests,” according to a government statement. “The Houthis’ renewed aggression targeting our partners and innocent civilians is unacceptable, and they must be held to account,” said Miliband. articles.preview: Several members of the group chat set up after the alleged murder of Feng Jianming say they or their parents were called by police from their home towns in China Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Chinese police have contacted several people who were part of a WeChat group that discussed attending a Melbourne vigil for Feng Jianming, the HungryPanda food delivery rider allegedly murdered earlier this month.
articles.body:
Chinese police have contacted several people who were part of a WeChat group that discussed attending a Melbourne vigil for Feng Jianming, the HungryPanda food delivery rider allegedly murdered earlier this month.

At least three members of the group set up after Feng’s death said they were contacted, raising concerns that Chinese authorities may have been alerted to discussions about the protest activity either automatically or manually by the Chinese-owned messaging and social app.

Feng was allegedly stabbed to death near Queen Victoria market on the evening of Friday 6 November after he and another rider confronted a man who was allegedly tampering with their bikes.

Angry members of the WeChat group set up in the immediate aftermath volunteered to host a vigil for the 49-year-old rider at the State Library of Victoria the following day, amid broader concerns about the treatment of riders by the company.

The group’s chat history, seen by the Guardian, shows that by Wednesday at least three members had told the group their parents or themselves had been called by police officers from their home towns in China asking about their involvement with the vigil. The group, which by then had more than 400 members, was disbanded the following day after participants expressed fears about the police calls.

Members of the chat group declined to speak on the record, citing safety concerns.

HungryPanda, founded in the UK, targets the Chinese expatriate market in 10 countries. In Australia, it operates in nine cities, including Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Adelaide.

The Melbourne incident mirrored an event in February when HungryPanda riders in Sydney were contacted by police from China after a WeChat discussion about a proposed strike over wages on lunar new year’s eve.

More than half the WeChat group’s 155 members left and the strike was abandoned after the calls from police, which were first reported by the ABC.

Joy Wang, a former HungryPanda rider who was in the February group chat, said she received four police calls from her home town in Henan province.

Wang said the police seemed unaware the protest was in Sydney. When she explained this, they threatened her with reprisals if she went back to China, she said.

“They said, ‘You better not attend the protest, or we could go after you when you return to China’,” Wang said.

Jack*, who quit HungryPanda two years ago and now runs his own business in eastern China, said he joined the February WeChat group to show support to his former colleagues. He received three calls from police in his home town and was told not to take part in the strike.

Jack then quit the group chat. “I’m currently in China, there are things I need to consider,” he said.

Kitty Lu, global spokeswoman for HungryPanda, said the company had no responsibility for riders being contacted by Chinese police. The company was privately owned and independently operated, with funding from private and institutional investors in Europe and North America, she said.

Wang said the group members in Australia who were called by police had registered with WeChat under their Chinese mobile numbers.

She believed the use of keywords such as “strike” in the chat may have been the trigger for the messages to be transmitted to the Chinese authorities.

Jeffrey Knockel, a senior research fellow at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, agreed. He and his colleagues studied a 2016 wage protest in Jiangsu province and found the phrase “industrial strike across the city” in the organisers’ group chat activated an automated mechanism on WeChat.

He suggested something similar may have happened in the Australian cases. Knockel also argued that WeChat may have flagged the group chat to a Chinese government organisation that would have then traced the riders’ details on China’s family registration system, known as hukou, and instructed local police to contact them.

WeChat has previously stated that the data of foreign users is stored in Singapore, beyond the reach of Chinese authorities, but Knockel said that if one member of a group registered their account with a Chinese number, the whole chat could be monitored by Chinese authorities.

WeChat did not respond to a request for comment.

Kevin Slaten, who leads the China Dissent Monitor at the US-based thinktank Freedom House, also thought the February calls might have been triggered by WeChat, given a rise in the number of labour disputes over wages in China during 2025 and early 2026.

“[The Chinese authorities may have] just assumed that these workers were in this wave of wage protests … not knowing initially that they weren’t physically located in China,” Slaten said.

But as the security apparatus was under direction to pay special attention to wage protests, the police may have persisted in warning riders to halt their action, even after learning they were overseas, he said.

The executive director of China Labor Watch, Qiang Li, has documented several cases of Chinese workers abroad being contacted by Chinese authorities after using WeChat to discuss industrial action. However, these workers were usually working for projects by China’s state companies.

Li said Chinese police had “overreacted” in the HungryPanda case but it was still alarming for Australia.

“Today we see these riders being called by Chinese police,” he said. “We could then see cases of anyone who uses WeChat, including Australian enforcement officials, their families, or anyone related to China, to be surveilled through this system.”

The home affairs department said it could not comment on operational matters but a spokesperson said it was “unacceptable for any foreign government to target members of our community to prevent individuals exercising their fundamental rights and freedoms in Australia”.

“Acts of harassment, assault, unwanted surveillance, intimidation, coercion or other threatening behaviour may constitute criminal offences.”

The opposition home affairs spokesman, Jonathon Duniam, called on the government to do more to address the potential use of WeChat for surveillance.

“The Coalition has raised serious concerns about WeChat’s links to the Chinese Communist party, its censorship practices and its potential use for surveillance, yet the Albanese government has not done enough to address these risks or ensure proper transparency and accountability from the platform,” he said.

In 2023, a Senate inquiry into foreign interference recommended banning WeChat on government devices and establishing a national security technology office to monitor “high-risk” social media groups, including WeChat.

The government said only that it “noted” these recommendations.

The Chinese embassy in Canberra declined to comment on the HungryPanda allegations.

articles.body:
Days out from the Victorian state election, the fate of nine datacentre projects remains uncertain, with some companies confident they will be able to get their projects across the line after Saturday.

There are nine datacentre projects currently awaiting approval according to the ministerial permits register, including the West Footscray expansion of NextDC’s M3 datacentre, which Guardian Australia reported has faced delays due to community blowback.

Other companies seeking approval for new datacentres include ZerraDC, HyperDC, GreenSquareDC, and Stockland.

The GreenSquareDC proposal for a $1.5bn, 240MW datacentre encompassing more than 105,000 sq metres of Spotswood in Melbourne’s inner west has faced strong opposition from locals similar to that observed in other suburbs around the country.

The proposal was lodged with the minister for planning at the end of July this year, but as with the other projects, it did not get approval before the government went into caretaker mode before the election.

A spokesperson for GreenSquareDC said the proposed development was on a long-vacant site in an established industrial precinct in Spotswood, and the company was proud of its proposal.

“We’ll work constructively with whichever government Victorians elect, and we’ll keep engaging with the Spotswood community throughout the process.”

Locals, however, have mobilised, with a petition with more than 4,400 signatures, and a dedicated website that encourages residents to contact the current planning minister and outlines the various policies on datacentres held by candidates in the Williamstown electorate.

The policies

Last month, after launching the Labor policy in September, the Victorian planning minister, Sonya Kilkenny, released a statement of expectations for applications submitted on or after 23 September.

It includes that datacentres must be built away from homes, schools, and childcare centres, and that they must be designed and located to minimise impact on residential communities.

Developments would be prohibited from residential zones, or within 150m of accommodation, education centres or hospitals, as well as green wedge zones (areas preserved for housing or agriculture), rural zones, or urban growth zones.

Exceptions on the latter are made if it is within 5km of a powerline or substation operating at 66,000 volts, or most of the electricity is supplied from either a renewable energy facility or a battery energy storage system.

Developers will be required to display prominent signage onsite and publish detailed application documentation online.

A spokesperson for the Coalition said datacentres would not be built in residential areas, next to residential areas, or in the green wedge.

“Datacentres will be an important part of Victoria’s future,” the spokesperson said. “They drive investment, create skilled jobs and build the sovereign capability our state needs in a digital economy.”

There would be designated datacentre precincts distanced from where people live, and clear guidelines on where they can and cannot be built, the spokesperson said.

“That means communities can have confidence their neighbourhoods are protected, and investors can have confidence about where to build.”

The Liberal policy does not outline whether the plans apply retrospectively, and makes no statement on power requirements.

The Victorian Greens have a policy of a moratorium on new datacentre developments “until communities have actually had an opportunity to consider the risks and benefits, and create strong laws to protect people and the planet over big tech profit”.

The party’s policy also calls for compensation for affected communities, reverting the fast-track approval process to give communities a greater say, and ensuring datacentres are 100% renewables-powered.

One Nation’s policies call for a ban on new datacentres on agricultural land, as well as a call for full community impact assessments before approval.

The party has also said there will be no retrospective carve-outs, so residents living next to a proposed or expanding datacentre will have the same rights as those living near new developments.

The party has also outlined that datacentres would need to be at an undefined distance from homes.

Developers confident ahead of the election

NextDC chief executive, Craig Scroggie, said in a shareholder update in late October that despite the issues with power supply to the datacentre, he had no reason to believe the expansion would not be approved after the election.

“Even with the revised changes to planning guidelines, they do not apply to existing applications that are already being considered by the planning minister.”

“This caretaker period will ultimately result in a new government being appointed [and a] new minister. We would therefore take the conservative view that given what we understand currently about the government’s approval processes and the upcoming election that the time we would be able to restart that [would be] February or later, depending on the election.”

Sean Brown, a West Footscray resident and Citizens of Tottenham member, told Guardian Australia last month the community would make its voice heard to the incoming planning minister after Saturday.

“We’re not stopping. This is continuing until we get a fair outcome for the residents,” he said.

“It will be a pretty toxic thing to sign off on.”

DoverDC, which is planning a $2.6bn 200MW datacentre next to AusNet’s South Morang terminal station, said its project would be assessed on its merits regardless of the election outcome.

“It is on this basis that it was accepted into the planning process by the current state government and we see no reason why that should change,” a spokesperson said.

Goodman Group, which has lodged plans for three two-storey datacentre buildings in Truganina, west of Melbourne, said it would not speculate on the election outcome or the planning decision but would work constructively with the government and local community.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed, seen from Egypt: A smear campaign reflecting the regime's anxiety
articles.summary: Since his election as a US senator in Michigan, the Democrat, a son of Egyptian immigrants, has come under fierce attack from most of Egypt's government-aligned media outlets, who accuse him of being close to the Muslim Brotherhood.

articles.body:
Three weeks after his resounding victory in the Senate race in Michigan during the midterm elections on November 3, Abdul El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants and now a leading figure of the Democratic Party's left wing, remains a hot topic along the Nile. While Egypt's authorities have yet to comment on the man who, come January 2027, will become the first Muslim US senator, the debate surrounding him is intense on social media and in the press.

Most media outlets, nearly all loyal to the regime, have worked hard to discredit the senator-elect, who, during his campaign, described President Abdel Fattah el-Sissi's government as "a military dictatorship funded by our tax dollars here." He was referring to the $1.3 billion in annual US aid to Washington's Arab ally, the second-largest recipient of US military assistance after Israel. The candidate argued that taxpayer money would be better spent on healthcare, schools and infrastructure than on foreign wars.

His stance alarmed Egypt's political and media elite, especially as the 42-year-old doctor-turned-politician won over a large segment of Arab public opinion with his quick wit and blunt criticisms of what he called the "genocide" in Gaza. Even Alaa Mubarak, son of former president Hosni Mubarak (1981-2011), posted a video of El-Sayed's victory speech, in which he addressed US Vice President JD Vance, one of his fiercest critics, with a friendly "habibi," an Arabic term of endearment.

Naim Abu Nahl, 50, was killed in a crowded area while four others, including a Palestinian woman, were wounded.

An Israeli strike on Gaza has killed a senior Hamas security official and wounded several others, according to local authorities.

In a statement, Gaza’s Ministry of Interior and National Security identified the official killed in Tuesday’s attack as Brigadier General Naim Abu Nahl, director of the Internal Security Service.

Abu Nahl was 50 years old and head of Hamas’s internal security across the Gaza Strip. A statement from Gaza’s Interior Ministry said the official was walking in the street when a drone strike killed him.

Four others, including a Palestinian woman, were wounded and taken to al-Shifa Medical Complex. The area where the missile struck is crowded with displaced people and shelters.

Hamas has condemned the assassination as a war crime, saying the killing is part of Israel’s efforts to create a “state of chaos” in the Gaza Strip.

“We affirm that these cowardly assassinations will not succeed in breaking the will of our people, nor will they deter our security and police forces from carrying out their national duty in protecting the internal front and preserving security and stability,” the group’s statement read.

Gaza’s Interior Ministry said the assassination came after the Internal Security Service had made significant gains against what it described as “gangs collaborating with the occupation and operating in areas under Israeli military control”.

Israel’s army and its Shin Bet domestic security service said in a joint statement that they had struck a senior Hamas figure, without identifying him, adding that further details would be provided later. Israel’s public broadcaster Kan later said the target was Abu Nahl. Citing Israeli sources, Kan said Abu Nahl had succeeded Moein al-Arbeid, who was detained by the Israeli army and Shin Bet during a special operation in September and remains in Israeli custody.

Several Palestinians were already reported killed earlier on Tuesday, including a child and police officers, while dozens were injured in Israeli air strikes on various parts of the Gaza Strip, according to local health officials.

There have been daily violations of the so-called “ceasefire” in Gaza, with Israeli air strikes continuing regularly in its genocidal war, with at least 1,680 people killed and 6,100 injured since the ceasefire was signed on October 11 last year.

Hamas also called on the guarantor states of the “ceasefire” agreement to intervene immediately “to rein in the occupation, impose a halt to its crimes, and obligate it to adhere to the agreement’s path”.

Prost said she had raised the transfers with British authorities and was considering asking whether the UK’s blocking statute could help her recover the money. The Canadian judge said one transfer was a wedding gift for a young couple and the other was a hotel payment. Both were sent from the Netherlands in euros to Britain in pounds. A US bank’s UK branch became involved in both transactions, she said. “In the United Kingdom, I have two instances where money was blocked and remains frozen,” Prost told journalists at the court’s headquarters in The Hague. “And this is the scenario, money sent from here in the Netherlands in euros to the United Kingdom in pounds, and I get an email which says: ‘Your money has been blocked on the basis of the order of the President of the United States, and if you want your money back, you must apply to the Office of Foreign Assets Control in the United States for a licence.’” In response to a request for comment, the UK foreign office did not address Prost's concerns. Instead, a source said that the UK "stands with the ICC" and is opposed to the sanctions. Her account sheds light on the personal toll of crippling US sanctions ahead of the ICC’s annual Assembly of States Parties, which opens in The Hague on 30 November. The meeting was moved from New York over concerns that sanctions and visa restrictions would limit participation. Washington sanctioned the court itself on 9 October, after targeting individual judges and prosecutors. 'The fact that [the US is] applying these measures is futile. I like to communicate that message, because we will not be intimidated' - Kimberly Prost, ICC judge The meeting comes amid criticism that member states have failed to match their public support for the court with practical protection for officials such as Prost. Washington's sanctions and threats to the ICC have been prompted by the Trump administration's opposition to the court's arrest warrant for Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the court's Afghanistan investigation which previously looked into US crimes. Washington has offered member states a six-month grace period to take measures that would address US demands to amend the court's treaty to prevent the prosecution of nationals of non-member states, like the US, Russia and Israel. Once fully in effect in April, the sanctions could stop the court from transacting in US dollars and potentially cripple its operations. Middle East Eye revealed on Monday that Guatemala had circulated a proposal urging talks with Washington on curbing the court’s ability to pursue nationals of countries outside the ICC, echoing US and Israeli demands. Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard accused Britain, Canada and other governments of seeking to appease Washington and called on them to act on their pledges to defend the court. ‘I have no regrets’ Washington sanctioned Prost in August 2025 over her role in a 2020 appeals ruling that authorised an investigation in Afghanistan, which could cover alleged crimes by US personnel. Asked about a recent decision to close that investigation and open a separate inquiry focused on the Taliban, Prost said she had questions about the decision herself and would wait to see the outcome of the appeal lodged by the Office of the Prosecutor against the decision. “I was sanctioned on the basis of my participation in the Appeals Chamber decision [to open the Afghanistan investigation], which I would make again today on the basis of the evidence that was in front of the Chamber,” she said. “I don’t know the state of the evidence today, only the prosecutor does. And I have no regrets about that decision whatsoever.” Kimberly Prost, ICC judge, speaks to journalists at the court's headquarters in The Hague on 19 November 2026 (MEE/Sondos Asem) Prost said the sanctions had left her without a credit card, made online shopping nearly impossible and stopped her from using Google Maps when she needed directions in London. She said, however, she is undeterred and that the pressure had no bearing on her work. “Independently and objectively, we look at the facts, the evidence, apply the law, and that’s the basis for our decision,” she said. “So the fact that they’re applying these measures is futile. I like to communicate that message, because we will not be intimidated.” She is one of three ICC judges who have sued the Trump administration over the sanctions . ‘Clear red lines’ Prost said British authorities had treated the frozen transfers as a decision for private industry. She disputed that the bank was obliged to block the funds and said she was considering asking about Britain’s blocking statute, a mechanism designed to counter certain foreign sanctions. Exclusive: Guatemala circulates proposal to curb ICC powers in line with US-Israeli demands e October sanctions against the court. “Now, in addition to those reactions and to the diplomacy, we need some strong measures being taken,” she said. She urged governments to use legal tools to tackle overcompliance and called for more public support from civil society and judicial associations. Prost, who helped negotiate the Rome Statute for Canada in 1998, said she supported dialogue with Washington but warned against putting the court’s jurisdiction up for negotiation. She was speaking about possible talks in general, without addressing Guatemala’s proposal specifically. “I mean, to me, that decision to include territorial jurisdiction was at the heart of the Rome Statute, and, in addition, it’s the will of those who participated in negotiations,” she said. “You can’t just change that because a group of states decide that it’s inconvenient at this point in time.” Under that principle, the court can pursue certain crimes committed on the territory of a member state regardless of the suspect’s nationality. Guatemala’s paper floated requiring the consent of the suspect’s country even when the alleged crimes took place in a member state. “One thing that cannot happen is this court cannot [be made to] stop,” Prost said. articles.summary: The two former leaders are facing accusations of complicity in financing terrorism and the acquisition of heavy weapons. The case centres on five Boeing 777s temporarily registered in Madagascar before being found in Iran in July 2025.
articles.preview: Andry Rajoelina Madagascar's anti-corruption prosecutors have requested arrest warrants for former president Andry Rajoelina and his former prime minister, Christian Ntsay, over a scandal involving five Boeing aircraft transferred to Iran. The two former leaders are facing accusations of complicity in financing terrorism and the acquisition of heavy weapons. articles.body:
Andry Rajoelina

Madagascar's anti-corruption prosecutors have requested arrest warrants for former president Andry Rajoelina and his former prime minister, Christian Ntsay, over a scandal involving five Boeing aircraft transferred to Iran.

The two former leaders are facing accusations of complicity in financing terrorism and the acquisition of heavy weapons. The case centres on five Boeing 777s temporarily registered in Madagascar before being found in Iran in July 2025.

Prosecutors say the aircraft were transferred to an Iranian airline under international sanctions. The latest proceedings have also brought 13 additional suspects into the case, with 11 placed in pre-trial detention.

The new charges also extend to 32 people already implicated in the first phase of the investigation.

Rajoelina and Ntsay left Madagascar in October 2025 after being removed from power. The requested arrest warrants must still be approved by an investigating judge.

The case marks a significant development in the investigation into the controversial transfer of the aircraft and the role of former government officials.

articles.title: UK sanctions Yemen’s Houthi group and four of its top officials
articles.summary: Group must be held accountable for 'targeting our partners and innocent civilians', says Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.
articles.preview: Group must be held accountable for ‘targeting our partners and innocent civilians’, says Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband. The United Kingdom has imposed sanctions on Yemen’s Houthis as well as four of the armed group’s senior officials. Announcing the measures on Wednesday, the British government accused the Iran-backed group of “deliberately attempting to undermine stability in the Middle East”.
articles.body:
Group must be held accountable for ‘targeting our partners and innocent civilians’, says Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.

The United Kingdom has imposed sanctions on Yemen’s Houthis as well as four of the armed group’s senior officials.

Announcing the measures on Wednesday, the British government accused the Iran-backed group of “deliberately attempting to undermine stability in the Middle East”.

It accused the four sanctioned individuals – Houthi Interior Minister Abdulkarim Amir al-Din Hussein al-Houthi, security and intelligence chief Abdul Hakim Hashem Ali al-Khaiwani, judge Mohammed Moufleh and prosecutor Sarim al-Din Muffadal – of involvement in human rights abuses.

Muffadal, according to the UK government, “is reasonably suspected of having directly perpetrated, or knowingly permitted or acquiesced in, sexual violence, including rape, torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment of women detainees”.

Al-Houthi, meanwhile, allegedly oversaw the custody of detainees who were “subjected to torture and other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment”. Such abuses included “electric shocks, beatings and sexual violence”, the UK government said.

The sanctioned individuals are subject to an asset freeze and travel ban, it added.

The UK government said the measures reaffirmed Britain’s view that “Houthi aggression is unacceptable and that the group must be held to account”.

It cited the group’s attacks on vessels in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, strikes targeting civil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and “aggression” in Yemen.

Since seizing Yemen’s capital Sanaa in September 2014, the Houthis – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – have controlled much of northern and western Yemen, and Yemen’s internationally recognised government has controlled much of the south. While a United Nations-brokered ceasefire largely halted the fighting in 2022, the conflict flared again in July when the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ports.

The group then carried out a lightning offensive in September, seizing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline near Bab al-Mandeb. UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the sanctions sent a message that Britain “will always act in support of British values and interests.”

“The Houthis’ renewed aggression targeting our partners and innocent civilians is unacceptable and they must be held to account,” said Miliband.

articles.summary: Andrei Chibis, head of Russia's northern Murmansk region, is the first governor to be detained for five years.

Andrei Chibis, 47, is suspected of embezzlement and misappropriation of more than a billion roubles ($12.2.m; £9.3m) set aside to build an Arctic highway, as well as a further 39m roubles from the Murmansk construction budget. articles.body:
The governor of Russia's northern Murmansk region has been arrested on corruption charges in the first detention of a regional leader for five years.

Andrei Chibis, 47, is suspected of embezzlement and misappropriation of more than a billion roubles ($12.2.m; £9.3m) set aside to build an Arctic highway, as well as a further 39m roubles from the Murmansk construction budget.

Chibis is reported to have been detained as he arrived on a visit to Moscow on Monday and was taken in for questioning.

He denies wrongdoing but has made no public comment. His wife Yevgenia Chibis said "anyone who knows our family understands how ridiculous this is".

In a post on social media, she said her husband sincerely believed in the Murmansk region and thanked people for their words of support: "We really need them right now."

Chibis worked for several years as deputy minister for construction and housing, before becoming governor of Murmansk in 2019.

Murmansk is a key military point for Russia in the Arctic and is home to the Russian navy's Northern fleet.

Chibis was re-elected two years ago after surviving a knife attack and is considered an active supporter of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Governors are seen as representing the Kremlin, and Vladimir Putin removed several in the months after the war began in February 2022.

However, until now no regional governor has been arrested since the start of the war, even though plenty of high-ranking officials have been detained in that time.

The Murmansk governor is one of a number of officials suspected of corruption by the Russian interior ministry's investigative department which, according to reports, alleged that a criminal group was set up in 2022 to embezzle money from the regional budget and move it abroad, including to Kyrgyzstan.

Another part of the case involves alleged fraud surrounding the rebuilding of a motorway between the two Arctic towns of Apatity and Kirovsk, which are 15km (9.3 miles) apart.

According to Russian news agency Interfax, a court will decide whether Chibis will remain in custody at a hearing on Wednesday.

He has been sanctioned by both the UK and EU, which accuses him of involvement in the illegal transportation of Ukrainian children to Russia and their adoption by Russian families.

articles.preview: Exclusive: Ada Colau hopes public anger over housing will transfer into support for her Broad Front coalition in Sunday’s vote The leader of Spain’s leftwing Broad Front coalition has called for a drastic rethink of the country’s entire housing rental system, and described the eviction of an 87-year-old woman – the spark for nationwide protests that in turn triggered Sunday’s snap general election – as “the last straw” for desperate tenants. “We’re not interested in small changes,” Ada Colau, the former Barcelona mayor, told the Guardian in an interview.
articles.body:
The leader of Spain’s leftwing Broad Front coalition has called for a drastic rethink of the country’s entire housing rental system, and described the eviction of an 87-year-old woman – the spark for nationwide protests that in turn triggered Sunday’s snap general election – as “the last straw” for desperate tenants.

“We’re not interested in small changes,” Ada Colau, the former Barcelona mayor, told the Guardian in an interview. “We want to reform the entire rental sector.”

Public outrage over the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid apartment in September prompted the government, led by Pedro Sánchez’s Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE), to propose a series of changes to Spain’s housing laws. After the proposals were voted down by a combination of rightwing parties and Catalan nationalists, Sánchez called an election.

“When Maricarmen, an 87-year-old woman who had paid rent all her life, was evicted out of pure greed, that lit the fuse,” said Colau, who stepped out of the political limelight three years ago after failing to win a third term as Barcelona mayor.

The Broad Front alliance was founded in February to unite parties to the left of the PSOE, and named Colau as its candidate for prime minister on 12 October. “When I saw how many people were taking to the streets that’s when I agreed to be a candidate,” she said. “I thought, if I can be useful now, I have to be involved 100%.”

Polls have indicated that the conservative People’s party (PP) will win the most seats in Sunday’s election, but will fall short of a parliamentary majority, meaning the far-right Vox party could become kingmakers. A coalition deal between the PP and Vox would signal the return of the far right to government in Spain for the first time in the country’s post-dictatorship democratic history.

Colau’s alliance does not include the leftist group Podemos or the Catalan Republican Left (ERC) party. “I said to both Podemos and ERC we could change the front’s name, I offered to stand aside in favour of a consensus candidate, but the parties decided on a different strategy and I have to respect their decision,” Colau said.

Colau said she was sceptical of polls pointing to a PP-Vox majority. “I don’t think the majority of people want to go back to pre-democratic times,” she said. “People in the street don’t share this fatalism that the political right is going to win.

“People are very motivated, they’re very conscious that this isn’t an election like any other. This is the first time since the dictatorship that the far right might be in government and we might see the return of censorship, that we might see something like ICE in Spain, as well as attacks on groups such as the LGBT community and women.”

Polls suggest that a broad leftwing coalition encompassing the PSOE and all the smaller parties to the left of it won’t get enough votes to secure a parliamentary majority, but Colau is undeterred. She pointed out that at the general election in 2023 it was predicted that the right and far right would win, only for voters to return a progressive government, “admittedly with a very mixed and rather fragile parliamentary majority”.

She added: “At the moment we’re at about 8% and our goal is 10%. We believe people want to vote not just to keep out the far right, they want to vote for social progress.”

Colau has been a housing activist for over 20 years, and says there is little to choose between the PP and PSOE on the issue, blaming both for the mortgage bubble that led to mass evictions after the 2008 financial crash and then allowing the current rental crisis to unfold.

“We’re not interested in small changes,” she said. “We want to reform the entire rental sector in line with something similar to Germany and, above all, get rid of the vulture funds that are destroying our neighbourhoods and driving us out of our cities. Vulture funds contribute nothing, everything they do is harmful.”

She said that 13 funds controlled about 100,000 properties, and that the Broad Front’s support for a Socialist-led government would depend on it agreeing to expropriate these properties “at a fair but not a market price”.

She said that when she was mayor she managed to increase the social housing stock by assuming control of more than 1,600 homes that were in the hands of big property owners. “If we could do that in Barcelona with fewer powers than the government, obviously it can be done at state level,” she said, adding that the constitution stated that housing was not only a right but that it must have a social function. “As for regulating rents, it isn’t such a radical proposal, it’s something that’s practised in various European countries.”

As mayor, Colau won international plaudits for her efforts to prioritise people over cars, but at home she was equally loved and loathed. During her time in office she came under constant attack from the pro-car lobby and faced over a dozen “lawfare” cases, all of which were rejected by the courts. Much of the hostility directed towards her was misogynist. “I’ve always said I’d only return to politics if I think I can be particularly useful, if not, I’ll do something else, because there are many ways to be political, not just in institutions,” she said. “If I can make a contribution now, I will do whatever I can to stop fascism returning to this country.”

articles.preview: The government conducted a crisis management drill assuming the first domestic Ebola case on Tuesday, in light of the World Health Organization’s international emergency declaration regarding the ongoing outbreak in Congo. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, related Cabinet members and the head of the Japan Institute for Health Security participated in the drill.
articles.body:
The government conducted a crisis management drill assuming the first domestic Ebola case on Tuesday, in light of the World Health Organization’s international emergency declaration regarding the ongoing outbreak in Congo.

The government has held an annual infectious disease response drill since 2023, and this year’s drill was the first to address the highly lethal disease.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, related Cabinet members and the head of the Japan Institute for Health Security participated in the drill.

During the drill, participants checked initial responses following an imaginary report that an Ebola patient had been confirmed in the southwestern prefecture of Fukuoka, which has an international airport.

The prime minister instructed officials to make every effort to prevent the virus from spreading, provide information based on scientific knowledge and ensure the safety and security of people.

Ebola has a fatality rate of 25% to 90% and can be transmitted through contact with a patient’s body fluids. In Japan, the disease is classified as the most dangerous category under the infectious disease control law.

In Congo, more than 5,500 people have died amid the Ebola outbreak since May.

articles.body:
Chen, 62, a member of the Communist Party's Politburo, is the first serving Shanghai boss to be placed under investigation since Chen Liangyu in 2006.

BEIJING: Shanghai's party chief Chen Jining, a member of the Communist Party's elite Politburo, is under investigation, China's state-run Xinhua news agency said on Tuesday (Nov 24), marking the fourth member of the top leadership body to be probed since 2025.

Chen is being investigated for "suspected severe violations of discipline and laws", Xinhua said. The phrase is a common euphemism for corruption.

He is the first serving Shanghai boss to be placed under investigation since Chen Liangyu in 2006.

Before the unexpected announcement of the Chen probe, three Politburo members from the 24-member body formed in 2022 - He Weidong, Zhang Youxia and Ma Xingrui - had already been removed.

The investigation of Chen marks a further escalation in President Xi Jinping's widening anti-graft campaign, which has thinned the party's senior leadership ranks and depleted the military's top command.

For Chinese officials, especially those of Chen's rank, the public announcement of an investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection generally signals their eventual political downfall.

Chen, 62, had an unusual rise through China's official ranks. An environmental scientist by training, he earned a doctorate from Imperial College London and rose through China's elite Tsinghua University to become its president.

He entered government as China's environmental protection minister before becoming mayor of Beijing. He joined the Politburo in 2022 and was named party boss of Shanghai, China's financial hub.

The Shanghai party secretary post is one of China's most prestigious provincial-level positions and has often served as a springboard to top leadership roles.

Xi, China's current leader, briefly served as Shanghai's party boss in 2007 before joining the Politburo's Standing Committee, the country's highest decision-making body.

China's second-ranking official, Premier Li Qiang, as well as Vice President Han Zheng, also held the Shanghai post before moving into central leadership roles.

articles.title: Car bomb tears through Colombian city wounding more than 20
articles.summary: The explosion is the latest in a string of attacks on buildings housing the security forces and government offices.
articles.preview: A car bomb has exploded in the central Colombian city of Villavicencio, injuring at least 23 people. The explosive device was detonated in front of the offices of the regional government, in the city centre, damaging several buildings. No group has so far admitted carrying out the attack - the latest in a series using explosives to target official buildings and security forces' headquarters. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella blamed "narcoterrorism", but gave no details.
articles.body:
A car bomb has exploded in the central Colombian city of Villavicencio, injuring at least 23 people.

The explosive device was detonated in front of the offices of the regional government, in the city centre, damaging several buildings.

No group has so far admitted carrying out the attack - the latest in a series using explosives to target official buildings and security forces' headquarters.

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella blamed "narcoterrorism", but gave no details. Armed criminal groups have recently stepped up attacks in what appears to be retaliation for an offensive ordered against them by De la Espriella.

Writing on social media, the president said that his government would "bluntly and forcefully" respond, external to "every drop of Colombian blood spilled".

"There will be no impunity and no retreat," he added.

Three weeks ago, three adults and a baby were killed in a car bomb attack near army barracks in Tolima province.

And earlier on Monday, drones dropped explosives on the police headquarters in the northern city of Cúcuta.

The car bomb in Villavicencio went off on Monday evening - the eve of the 10th anniversary of the signing of a peace deal between the government and left-wing rebels of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc), Colombia's largest guerrilla group.

Following the signing of the deal, thousands of left-wing rebel fighters laid down their arms.

However, a significant number of Farc members, who did not agree with the deal, refused to disarm and joined dissident groups instead.

While forced displacement, child recruitment and the numbers of attacks on security forces dropped in the aftermath of the deal, there has been an upsurge in recent years driven by dissident Farc factions and criminal groups fighting for control of drug trafficking, illegal mining and extortion rackets.

Colombia's first left-wing president, who was in power from August 2022 to August 2026, tried to negotiate with these armed groups as part of what he called his "total peace" strategy.

However, the talks stalled and collapsed with several of the criminal groups violating ceasefires they had agreed to observe.

De la Espriella was elected on a promise to crack down on "narcoterrorism" and has been scathing about his predecessor's approach.

He has also been critical of the 2016 agreement, calling it a "false peace".

In a post on X, uploaded shortly before news of the car bomb in Villavicencio spread, he referred to the peace deal as a "mess", describing it as a "waste of public resources" and the "cause behind Colombia's ruin".

Former President Juan Manuel Santos and Rodrigo Londoño - the two men who signed the peace deal on behalf of the Colombian government and the Farc respectively - defended it in an interview with BBC Mundo ahead of the anniversary.

Santos said that De la Espriella was "totally wrong" to call it a "false peace".

"He wants to use, or has bought into that cynical and mistaken theory that the violence we see today is the result of the peace deal, when the exact opposite is the case," Santos said, arguing that the problem lies with the lack of implementation of the agreement.

articles.title: Land mine casualties soar in Syria, two years after war
articles.summary: Nearly 1,000 children are among those killed or injured by explosives left over from the conflict, figures show.
articles.preview: Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang. "Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC. Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured. Unwittingly, the children had triggered a landmine.
articles.body:
Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang.

"Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.

Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured.

Unwittingly, the children had triggered a landmine.

The incident and others this week bring to nearly 1,000 the number of children killed or injured by explosive ordnance in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, according to the UN Mine Action Service (Unmas).

The village is one of many where families have returned to homes and farmland that were once on the front lines of Syria's 13-year civil war.

Alaa's father said demining teams had visited several times to clear the fields. He and other residents believed it was safe for farmers and children to move around.

But mines and other explosives can lie far beyond former battle lines, making it difficult to establish which areas are safe.

"Remnants of war from today's conflicts are often very widely and broadly scattered, often without patterns, which makes it extremely difficult to do clearance," Katrin Atkins, research lead at Landmine Monitor, a global mine monitoring initiative, told the BBC.

The dangers are reflected in a sharp rise in casualties across Syria.

A total of 1,602 people were killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war in 2025 alone, an increase of more than 50% on the previous year, according to the Landmine Monitor report, published by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines on Tuesday.

Only Myanmar, with 1,891 casualties, recorded more.

The report attributes the rise in Syria partly to the large-scale return of refugees and internally displaced people following Assad's overthrow.

"When you look at population movement, a couple of months later you see an increase of incidents in these areas, because that's exactly where people go and start to use the fields again," Atkins said.

More than 60% of casualties recorded by the world's largest landmine clearance charity, the Halo Trust, involve farming, agriculture or shepherding, according to its Syria programme manager, Simon Jackson.

"They're not going to wait for the government or for organisations like us to come and tell them that everything is safe and clear," he told the BBC. "People are taking risks out of desperation."

Since Assad's fall on 8 December 2024, Unmas has recorded at least 1,556 incidents in Syria involving explosive ordnance.

They have caused 2,701 casualties: 935 people killed and 1,766 injured. Children account for 995 of those victims, or about 37%.

But the toll is likely to be higher, with experts estimating that overall casualties could be under-reported by 25-50%.

For many of those who survive, the consequences are devastating and permanent.

Majid Abdul Rahman, 27, was travelling in a car in the Ghouta region on the outskirts of Damascus in March 2025 when it struck an explosive device. The vehicle filled with smoke and he felt a pain in his leg.

More than a year later, Majid has difficulty walking and has been unable to return to work, leaving him struggling to provide for his family.

The danger has continued into this month, with at least 20 people killed and more than 40 injured by explosive ordnance in November.

In one of the worst recorded incidents, an explosion in a school courtyard in Hasakah on 4 November killed a 12-year-old and injured 19 others. And on Monday, a 13-year-old boy was killed when an unexploded cluster munition detonated in southern Daraa province.

The threat is also holding back Syria's economic recovery. Contaminated farmland cannot be safely cultivated, while people collecting scrap metal or trying to salvage materials from abandoned areas also risk triggering explosions.

The Syrian Ministry of Defence says since the end of 2024 its teams have found and dealt with more than 315,000 mines and unexploded munitions.

But no nationwide survey has established how much land remains contaminated, making it difficult to assess the full scale of the problem.

"We're in a bit of a black hole," Atkins said.

And with the extent of contamination still largely unknown, the war continues to claim victims two years after it ended.

The opposition is expected to challenge the measure in the country’s Constiutional Court if/when it is signed into law by Slovakia’s president, Peter Pellegrini.

The prime minister, Robert Fico, has claimed the legislation was intended to “prevent fraud and manipulations”, without providing evidence.

Rejecting this justification, the opposition argue the measure targets pro-western voters and would unfairly prevent tens of thousands of Slovaks from exercising their democratic right to vote.

“They are afraid that voters will give them a bill in the (parliamentary) September elections, so they have preventively prevented a large part of voters from expressing their opinion,” Michal Šimečka, leader of the major opposition Progressive Slovakia party, was quoted as having said.

Zelenskyy confirms Ukraine hit Russian cargo ship in Gulf of Finland

Simon Tisdall

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed that Ukraine was responsible for Saturday’s drone strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland, Bloomberg News reported.

Zelenskyy told Bloomberg in an interview that the vessel, Sparta II, had been a legitimate target for his military as it was carrying weapons.

“Every vessel with a Russian flag, everything that carries weapons or any sanctioned cargo that can carry God knows what, it is a legitimate target for us in Russian territorial or neutral waters.”

The vessel, operated by the Russian defence logistics firm Oboronlogistika, was hit in international waters in the Gulf of Finland. One crew member was injured.

Bloomberg noted that it could not independently verify Zelenskyy’s claims that the ship was carrying weapons.

Nato's Rutte to meet US president Trump on Wednesday

Meanwhile, Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte will travel to Florida to meet the US president, Donald Trump, at Mar-a-Lago on Wednesday, the alliance said.

Rutte “will also meet with senior administration officials,” Nato said.

The pair last met in July at Nato’s summit in Ankara.

Norway’s defence minister Tore Sandvik told reporters there is an ongoing dialogue with Ukraine regarding “a need for stability in our near areas”.

Finland’s military on Saturday said that a drone strike on a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea was likely carried out by Ukraine.

“All attacks would stop immediately if Russia stopped this war. Once that is said, we are focused on the fact that Ukraine must do this inside the rules of international law. So we take this up with them,” Sandvik told a press conference.

“We are also focused on the fact that they must respect our need for stability in our near area and we have a good dialogue with the Ukrainians on that now.”

'Situation with power supply is difficult,' Zelenskyy says as Russian strikes continue

Back to Ukraine, the country’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that “the situation with power supply is difficult” amid continuing Russian strikes against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

He stressed, however, that “the necessary personnel and resources have been mobilized for restoration.” “It is important to speed up the work.”

Zelenskyy also held talks with energy minister “on the implementation of the steps we agreed upon to increase electricity generation and accelerate the restoration of energy facilities following Russian strikes,” and with defence minister “on the use of our long-range weapons and the preparation of new support packages from our partners,” he said.

Sweden remains stuck in government talks as 'no conditions' to from centre-left administration

Over in Sweden, election winner Magdalena Andersson has repeated that there are still “no conditions” for her to form a new centre-left government, SVT reported.

72 days on from the election, Sweden is still unable to confirm a new government, with the speaker, Andreas Norlén, increasingly running out of patience.

The four centre-left parties remain deadlocked as the Left party and the Centre party keep making conflicting demands on the government’s composition.

The Centre party, which previously favoured discussions with Andersson, has now resumed talks with the centre-right bloc, led by the incumbent prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, about teaming up to form the next government.

The task of exploring potential majorities now rests with Kristersson, after two failed attempts by Andersson (Europe Live, 15 October) and the Centre party’s leader, Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist (3 November) with a third vote – on Kristersson - expected in the coming days.

Norlén said last week that he wanted to exhaust the process – with four votes – before Christmas, either getting a new government in place or calling a snap election to break the standoff (Europe Live, last week).

After the 2018 election, it took 134 days to form a government, so the current process is still some way off that record.

Hungary's Magyar to meet Zelenskyy, visit Ukraine border region inhabited by ethnic Hungarians

Meanwhile, Hungary’s prime minister Péter Magyar announced a visit to the border region of Transcarpathia for talks with Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Announcing the visit on Facebook, Magyar said:

“Together with [foreign] minister Anita Orbán, we will visit several Hungarian institutions. This is the first visit by a Hungarian prime minister to Ukraine since 2015.”

The region, inhabited by some 60,000 ethnic Hungarians, has been one of the flashpoints in relations between Hungary and Ukraine under the previous government of Viktor Orbán.

But the visit comes just days after Hungary dropped its opposition to opening of the remaining “clusters” in Ukraine’s talks on accession to the EU,as reported by Euronews, with Magyar seeking a more constructive relationship with Ukraine.

US delaying delivery of much-needed Patriot air defence missiles - media report

Meanwhile, the Financial Times is reporting this morning that the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of about 60 much-needed Patriot air defence interceptors to Ukraine.

The interceptors, paid for by Ukraine’s western allies, are reportedly being held up by the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, who needs to sign off on their re-export, three people told the newspaper.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has repeatedly warned of the urgent need for more air defence missiles to protect the skies above Ukraine as the country braces for a difficult winter, with Russia continuing its strikes on critical civilian infrastructure.

The drone, believed to be carrying surveillance equipment, remained in Polish airspace for eight minutes before flying back to Ukraine.

Poland’s deputy defence minister, Paweł Zalewski, told RMF24 that the military decided against shooting it down because of risks to civilian properties in the area.

The incident took place just hours after Nato held emergency talks over last week’s airspace breach, authorising the deployment of a Nato Airborne Warning and Control System, AWACS, aircraft to Poland.

Overnight, at least two people were killed and 40 injured in Russian attacks on the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, with further attacks reported in the Sumy region.

articles.title: How the Iran war is reshaping the US military presence in the Middle East
articles.summary: Experts say fallout from the war and domestic opposition could force a smaller permanent presence in the Middle East.
articles.preview: Experts say fallout from the Iran war and domestic opposition could force a smaller permanent presence in the Middle East. The United States military presence across the Middle East is sprawling. There are as many as 50,000 US troops and about 19 major military installations in the region, as well as assets spread across countries such as Bahrain, Jordan and Saudi Arabia.
articles.body:
Experts say fallout from the Iran war and domestic opposition could force a smaller permanent presence in the Middle East.

The United States military presence across the Middle East is sprawling.

There are as many as 50,000 US troops and about 19 major military installations in the region, as well as assets spread across countries such as Bahrain, Jordan and Saudi Arabia.

But experts warn that the US-Israel war on Iran has exposed vulnerabilities in protecting Washington’s military assets in the region, leading some to speculate that a downsizing may occur once the war is over.

Michael O’Hanlon, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a Washington-based think tank, is among those who expect the US to eventually scale back its military presence in the Middle East.

“I think we will go smaller, more dispersed, more hardened, and generally further away from Iran — but not in each and every case,” O’Hanlon said.

As the war enters its 10th month on Saturday, the damage inflicted on US installations in the Middle East could one day translate into a strategic shift — not just for the US but for other countries that have been shaped by its military presence as well.

Billions of dollars in damage

One of the long-term obstacles to maintaining the US military presence will be the cost of repairs.

Repairing damaged infrastructure on US bases in the region could cost $9.4b, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington, DC-based think tank.

Hundreds of structures on US bases have been damaged by Iranian attacks since February 28, when the war began.

One of those bases was in Bahrain, home to the US Naval Forces Central Command and its Fifth Naval Fleet. The US has established a naval command presence in the country as far back as 1948.

But according to a report from the Congressional Research Service, the base — called Naval Support Activity (NSA) Bahrain — “sustained serious damage” in the early days of the Iran war. It estimated the cost of repairing the base at more than $400m.

Other US military assets in the region have also been impacted by the war.

In September, a Department of Defense inspector general report found the US had lost dozens of aircraft during the war, among them attack helicopters and sophisticated fighter jets like the F-35A and the F-15E.

By October, the total cost of the Iran war reached more than $47bn, according to Pentagon figures.

Rethinking the need for large bases

Rebuilding the US bases is unlikely until the Iran war is over, according to Mark Cancian, a senior adviser with the Defense and Security Department at CSIS.

“If the war ends with some sort of ceasefire or we get to a place where it’s somewhat stable,” Cancian said, “then you will see some reduction in US forces and reduction of the surge forces certainly and some rebuilding of the bases.”

But Cancian expects that the US will not rebuild all the military sites struck by Iran.

He pointed to the Bahrain headquarters of the Fifth Naval Fleet and the Combined Air Operations Center at Al Udeid airbase in Qatar as examples.

Some military facilities, he explained, will likely be moved underground to protect against aerial attack. Others may be relocated further from the Gulf, to places such as Israel or Jordan.

Major bases like those in Bahrain or Qatar were a liability because “they are right within the range of Iranian missiles and drones”, according to Kelly Grieco, a defence policy expert and senior fellow at the Stimson Center, a global security think tank.

But simply moving bases further away will not protect them in the long term. Grieco pointed out that Iran keeps improving its ability to reach longer-distance targets with drones and missiles.

One alternative to rebuilding bases, she said, would be instead to cultivate access to a network of airstrips and temporary bases in the Middle East that could be used if another conflict erupts.

In the Iran war, for instance, the US has relied extensively on facilities like Israel’s Ben Gurion airport for refuelling combat aircraft.

“What mattered more was access to places and the ability to move around those places, more than having a permanent operating facility,” Grieco said.

What the region wants

Experts say downsizing the US military presence in the Middle East has been a goal across several administrations.

President Donald Trump, for instance, has completed troop withdrawals from Syria and Iraq since the start of his second term in 2025. His predecessor, Joe Biden, also oversaw the US military pullout from Afghanistan in 2021.

But practical realities — including the emergence of new conflicts involving the US — have put that aspiration of a large-scale drawdown out of reach.

“The Biden administration wanted to reduce the force posture. The Trump administration wanted to reduce the force posture,” Cancian said. “They haven’t been able to, and it’s not clear they will be able to.”

Allies and adversaries alike also help to determine the heft of the US military presence, he added.

“The world gets a vote, and even if the administration wants to reduce the force posture, it may not be possible, because of continuing tensions,” Cancian said.

New alliances, however, have emerged that might make certain regional allies less reliant on US military resources.

In August, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, a pact that theoretically commits the countries to come to each other’s aid in case of an attack.

Experts say the deal could trigger a regional realignment away from the US and its military might.

Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan could potentially wield formidable force: Together, they have more than 1.4 million active military personnel, own thousands of tanks and military aircraft and spend more than $124bn on their combined defence budget.

The pact is also likely to expand to include Egypt and Syria, further increasing its resources.

Such agreements might prove to be the first step in diversifying each country’s military strategy beyond their cooperation with the US, according to Grieco.

“The region had already been engaged in strategic diversification before this war started,” she said. “The real question moving forward is: Will they decide to pursue greater strategic dependence, or slowly decrease their dependence on the US for security?”

Domestic frustrations grow

In the US, voter frustration could also disincentivise any effort to rebuild military installations in the Middle East.

The Iran war and US support for Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza have proven to be unpopular among the American public.

This month, for instance, the research firm Ipsos and the Reuters news agency found that 71 percent of Americans wanted Congress to end the war on Iran.

The conflict proved especially unpopular at the polls, with Trump’s Republican Party losing key races in the 2026 midterms to Democrats who were vocal in their opposition.

There was even backlash from within Republican ranks. Vice President JD Vance, who once touted his opposition to foreign wars, blamed the Iran conflict for his party’s poor showing in the midterm elections.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so,” Vance wrote on social media. “Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

Both parties are leaning away from a foreign interventionist stance, according to Grieco.

Although politicians are split over topics like US support for Israel, Grieco has observed that there is an overall inclination to extricate the US military from the Middle East.

“For most Americans, they’ve looked at the region since 1990 or 1991 and seen we are constantly conducting these interventions,” Grieco said. “None of them have gone well.”

articles.title: Yemen ministry puts losses from Saudi attacks and blockade above $1.13 trillion
articles.summary: Yemen ministry puts losses from Saudi attacks and blockade above $1.13 trillion Yemen’s Houthi-run Economy Ministry says Saudi attacks and the blockade have inflicted more than $1.13 trillion in cumulative economic losses since the war began began in March 2015. Acting Economy Minister Sam al-Bashiri said preliminary estimates put direct damage during the latest escalation, from 13 July to 23 November, at more than $881.5m, Saba reports. He said Saudi strikes destroyed 22 factories and partially damaged three others, causing industrial losses exceeding $376m. The ministry put commercial losses above $85m and investment-sector losses above $20m. Transport and Public Works Minister Mohammed Quhaim reported more than $350m in damage to infrastructure and other sectors during the same period. Quhaim said attacks on airports, ports, roads and bridges had disrupted supplies and increased shipping, insurance and storage costs, placing further financial pressure on Yemenis. The announcement provided no detailed methodology for the cumulative trillion-dollar estimate.

articles.body:
11 injured after ‘unspecified projectile’ hits tower in Riyadh

The Saudi-led coalition says building in financial district targeted, marking second time in a week.

11 people have been injured after an unspecified projectile struck a tower Riyadh’s financial district, according to Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence agency.

Those injured include two Saudi citizens, two Indian nationals, three Nepali nationals and four Egyptian nationals, a civil defence spokesperson said.

Authorities said emergency services responded immediately and took the necessary measures to protect civilian lives and property.

In a post on the social media platform X, the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition called the Tuesday strike targeting the King Abdullah Financial District a “cowardly terrorist attack”, adding that authorities are conducting an on-site investigation.

The strike marks the second attack on Riyadh’s financial district in less than a week. An earlier attack on Riyadh damaged the Public Investment Fund (PIF) tower, the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund and the country’s tallest skyscraper. The strike caused “material damage”.

The Saudi-led coalition has not named the building that was struck on Tuesday. However, three separate witnesses said a strike targeted the PIF skyscraper.

A fourth witness told the news agency AFP that a vehicle fitted with a speaker had warned pedestrians in the area to take cover.

No warning was sent to phones about any threats to the capital, as has been the case during recent strikes.
